questions.answer: We need to reverse the chain rule. Let \(u=x^2+5\). Then \(du=2x\,dx\), which appears in the integral. The integral becomes \(\int u^4\,du\). Integrate: \(\frac{u^5}{5}+C\). Substitute back: \(\frac{(x^2+5)^5}{5}+C\).

We need a substitution for the inner linear expression. Let \(u=3x+1\). Then \(du=3\,dx\), so the integral becomes \(\int u^7\,du\). Integrate: \(\frac{u^8}{8}+C\). Substitute back to get \(\frac{(3x+1)^8}{8}+C\).

We need a definite integral with substitution. Let \(u=x^2\), so \(du=2x\,dx\). Change the limits: when \(x=0\), \(u=0\); when \(x=1\), \(u=1\). The integral becomes \(\int_0^1 e^u\,du\). An antiderivative is \(e^u\), so the value is \(e^u\big|_0^1=e-1\).

We need a substitution for the denominator. Let \(u=x^2+9\). Then \(du=2x\,dx\). The integral becomes \(\int\frac{1}{u}\,du\). The antiderivative is \(\ln|u|+C\). Since \(u=x^2+9>0\), the answer is \(\ln(x^2+9)+C\).

We need to account for the inner derivative of \(5x\). Let \(u=5x\). Then \(du=5\,dx\), so \(dx=\frac{1}{5}\,du\). The integral becomes \(\frac{1}{5}\int\cos u\,du\). Since \(\int\cos u\,du=\sin u\), the answer is \(\frac{1}{5}\sin(5x)+C\).

We need the inner expression under the square root. Let \(u=x^2+4\). Then \(du=2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx=\frac{1}{2}du\). The integral becomes \(\frac{1}{2}\int u^{1/2}\,du\). Integrate: \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{u^{3/2}}{3/2}=\frac{1}{3}u^{3/2}\). Substitute back: \(\frac{1}{3}(x^2+4)^{3/2}+C\).

We need a substitution for \(2x+1\). Let \(u=2x+1\), so \(du=2\,dx\) and \(dx=\frac{1}{2}du\). Change limits: when \(x=1\), \(u=3\); when \(x=2\), \(u=5\). The integral becomes \(\frac{1}{2}\int_3^5\frac{1}{u}\,du\). This equals \(\frac{1}{2}[\ln u]_3^5=\frac{1}{2}(\ln5-\ln3)=\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{5}{3}\).

We need a substitution for \(1-x^2\). Let \(u=1-x^2\). Then \(du=-2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx=-\frac{1}{2}du\). The integral becomes \(-\frac{1}{2}\int u^{-1/2}\,du\). Integrate: \(-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2u^{1/2}=-\sqrt{u}\). Substitute back to get \(-\sqrt{1-x^2}+C\).

We need to use the derivative of \(1+\cos x\). Let \(u=1+\cos x\). Then \(du=-\sin x\,dx\), so \(\sin x\,dx=-du\). Change limits: when \(x=0\), \(u=2\); when \(x=\pi\), \(u=0\). The integral becomes \(-\int_2^0 u^3\,du=\int_0^2 u^3\,du\). Evaluate: \(\frac{u^4}{4}\big|_0^2=\frac{16}{4}=4\). Therefore the integral is \(4\).

questions.prompt: Find \(\int \tan x\,dx\) by writing \(\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\).
questions.answer: We need to integrate \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Let \(u=\cos x\). Then \(du=-\sin x\,dx\), so \(\sin x\,dx=-du\). The integral becomes \(-\int\frac{1}{u}\,du\). This equals \(-\ln|u|+C\). Substitute back: \(-\ln|\cos x|+C\), which is also \(\ln|\sec x|+C\).
